reply_line: To answer, reply “As recommended”, or name the item and your change.

panels.title: Board 1 drawings that changed
panels.lede: Three drawings you approved on board 1 changed in rounds 2 and 3: S12, S16 and S10. Eleven board 1 drawings, S12 and S16 among them, moved a word, label or key at widths board 1 did not show, and twelve round 1 charts changed the words that name an ink. We recommend one approval for the lot, with S12 kept in its scrolling frame.

items.title: S12, the shift arrows map at a desk
items.answer: Board 1 approved S12 drawn 1,024 px wide. The guide's column is narrower than that at every desk width, so the approved drawing now sits in a frame 1,024 px wide that scrolls sideways. From a 1,280 px window the frame widens over the chapter list on the left. The other choice is a tile that sets each state's code and figure on two lines with the arrow under them, which fits a column 723 px wide or more.
items.what_changed: At a 1,440 px window the frame shows 943 of the drawing's 1,024 px, from Alaska to New Jersey and Connecticut, with New York, Florida and California in view; the column with Maine and Rhode Island needs a scroll, and a line above the map says so. At a 1,024 px window the column shows about 558 px, a little over half. While S12 is in view the chapter list on the left is hidden. On a phone S12 draws gray steps, as board 1 approved, and now prints each state's code where its tile holds it.
items.why: Board 1's arrows need tiles 72 px wide, which only a drawing 930 px wide or more gives. Chapter 14 never gives a drawing that width, so the round 3 reviewers found S12 drawing gray steps at every desk width, with no arrows, though its entry, reading guide and alt describe arrows.
items.recommendation: Keep the 1,024 px frame as built. It shows the drawing you approved, unchanged, at every desk width, and the four states the title names are in view at 1,440 px. The stacked tile fits only from a 723 px column, so a 1,024 px window would still need the scrolling frame, and the guide would carry two desk drawings of one chart.

views.text: Keep the 1,024 px frame as built: it is board 1's drawing unchanged, and at 1,440 px only the column with Maine and Rhode Island sits past the edge. Take the stacked tile only if you want the whole map in view at 1,440 px with the chapter list kept, knowing a 1,024 px window still scrolls.

S12's stage: the arrows draw, but at a 1440 px desk a reader sees about 70 percent of the map and must scroll to reach the title's eastern states. Board 2 should show the scrolling stage beside the stacked tile, which keeps board 1's encoding and fits the column from 723 px.
views.note: Written before the frame widened over the chapter list (D3-1515), when 723 of the 1,024 px showed at 1,440 px.

items.title: S16, the turnout bubble map
items.answer: S16 now draws on the Census Bureau's 2024 state outlines, with Alaska and Hawaii framed apart, DC on a leader at a desk, every state's code on a phone, a credit line for the map, and the range words you approved on November 13. Its data, circle sizes, inks and named states are as board 1 approved.
items.what_changed: The 2024 outlines, with the coast drawn as an edge; Alaska and Hawaii each in a frame, not to scale; DC on a leader at a desk and West Virginia beside its own circle; codes placed so that at a 358 px phone drawing all 51 carry a code, where board 1's named two in a note; a credit line naming the map's source; note 3's range and the alt's last sentence in the words of DR-256.
items.why: Round 3 moved every state map onto one set of 2024 outlines, and the reviewers asked for DC and the small northeastern states to be findable. Placement only: the data, the circle scale and its key, the inks, the title, the notes but note 3, and the table are unchanged.

items.title: S10, the evidence mix bars
items.answer: S10's bar for all 433 claims now draws as a dashed line in the text's ink with its own label, the way every total or national line in chapter 14 draws (Rule 14.6). Nothing else in the drawing moved.
items.what_changed: The overall line, “All 433 claims”, is a dashed total line.
items.why: One treatment for a total line across the chapter.

items.title: Eleven board 1 drawings moved a word or a label at widths board 1 did not show
items.answer: A width check now draws every chart at every width from 256 px up, and a crossing check finds words that touch a line. Eleven board 1 drawings moved a word, a label or a key where those checks found a fault. No figure, ink or word changed.
items.what_changed: Each row says what moved. Unless the row says otherwise, the 1,440 and 390 px drawings board 1 showed are unchanged.
items.why: At some widths a label ran past the edge or across a line.

rows.what_changed: Takes its phone arrangement wherever “86%” would reach the bars beside it, and a party's words move under the bar where the 60-vote line would cross them.
Its two notes move under the chart below 620 px (2025) and 510 px (2021), as on a phone.
Gridlines draw before the panel words, and each bracket's words after its lines.
The year line sits in from the left, and only where the tile holds it with 2 px each side.
Each label is measured at the width it is drawn and may wrap at six more widths; the drawing differs at 558 px only.
The center line draws before the rows, and the bottom scale drops a figure that would touch its neighbor; the same figures sit at the same places.
On a phone each tile prints its state's code where the tile holds it, and a note names the codes with no room; under 292 px the table names every state.
A one-word panel name wider than its panel stays inside the drawing.
The “Three-month average” note sits 10 px higher at every desk width and moves to the key under 490 px.
The “Leader changed” tag goes under the state's name on a phone where it would reach the shift column.
The size key drops under the shade key where it would run past the edge.

items.answer: The notes and alt text of twelve round 1 charts now name a mark the same way on both grounds: the mark the title names is “in the text’s ink”, other marks are “gray”, and no ink is called dark or light. No drawing changed.
items.what_changed: The words that name inks in each chart's notes, alt text and reading guide.
items.why: Dark and light swap on Charcoal, so “dark ink” was wrong on one ground.

panels.title: Forms whose tier or data changed
panels.lede: No form changed its tier. Nine specimens changed their data, measure or drawing after their data plan row was signed off, each for a reason a review found, and seventeen changes were made to the data plans before anything was fetched. We recommend one approval for the list.

items.title: Tiers
items.answer: No form changed its tier. All 114 forms of rounds 1 to 3 carry the tier the coverage plan gave them: 50 core, 36 extended, 21 reference and 7 to avoid.
items.why: A script read each form's tier in the coverage plan, the chapter 14 plan, the data plans, each entry and each spec.

items.title: S73, the joint fundraising committees
items.answer: S73 now draws every committee the Federal Election Commission designates a joint fundraising committee that paid either party's 2024 presidential campaign: three on the Democratic side and four on the Republican side, in place of one each.
items.what_changed: The plan picked the one committee per nominee that sent the campaign the most. The chart now reads all seven by that rule, from a new file, with transfers to other committees (line 22) as the measure for both. The Democratic campaign and its main fund carried Joseph R. Biden Jr.'s name until July 21, 2024, so the line under that bar names both candidates with the date, and a note splits that side's transfers before and after the date. The Republican side kept one candidate and is not split; its two renames are named with their dates.
items.why: Read from the right, picking one committee per side drew a contrast in reach (53 committees against two) that came from the rule, not from the record. Read across all seven, both sides reached a similar number of committees: 54 and 56.

plan_row.said: `fec-jfc-transfers-2024`: the one committee per nominee that transferred the most to the nominee's principal campaign committee (data lead change 8).

items.built: `fec-jfc-transfers-2024-all-committees` (research ledger P7-226): all seven designated joint fundraising committees, line 22, refunds on line 28C set apart.

items.title: S76, where 2024 House campaign money came from and went
items.answer: S76 now nets the transfers between each campaign and its own other committees candidate by candidate, and draws the money sent out as its own band.
items.what_changed: The file had netted transfers across all 1,926 campaigns at once, which left $156.8 million in and nothing out. Netted for each candidate, $175.1 million came in and $18.3 million went out. The money left unaccounted for stays $1.5 million, and a note says 297 campaigns' figures do not balance, with one campaign leaving nearly all of it.
items.why: Netting across campaigns cancels one campaign's money out against another's money in, and those dollars never met. The note promised candidate-by-candidate netting.

plan_row.said: Transfers between a candidate's own committees are netted out.

items.built: `fec-house-campaigns-2024-money-in-out`, transfers netted candidate by candidate (research ledger P7-217).

items.title: S78, broadband by state
items.answer: S78 maps home broadband such as cable, fiber or DSL, a line of the Census Bureau's table the plan left open, with the Bureau's own published margins, and on a phone it draws the studio's tile grid in place of state outlines.
items.what_changed: The plan asked for “households with a broadband internet subscription”. The chart reads the table's fixed broadband line, which leaves out a household with a cellular data plan alone, and prints the margins the Bureau publishes. Under 520 px the map becomes the tile grid S07 uses, with the same classes, inks and key, so every state carries its code.
items.why: The atlas issue it serves (I015) names slow or missing home internet, which a phone plan alone does not answer, and broadband of any kind spans too narrow a range for more than two honest classes. On the outlines, 19 states had no room for a code at a 358 px phone drawing.

plan_row.said: Households with a broadband internet subscription, table B28002, with margins; the line used to be named.

items.built: B28002's fixed broadband line, with the published margins of table S2801 (source variant `fixed_with_s2801_margin`).

items.title: S80, Michigan's House districts
items.answer: S80 now draws a framed inset of the Detroit area in both panels, so the five districts there are large enough to number and read.
items.what_changed: The 6th and the 10th to 13th districts draw again, larger, in a framed inset in each panel, and a note says each district elects one member whatever its area. The margin steps on S80 and S82 moved from gray to four steps of Verdigris.
items.why: Land stood in for seats: the small Detroit districts were too small to see, and gray step 1 read as the other party's empty seat.

plan_row.said: Michigan's 13 districts with the district geometry.

items.built: The same results and geometry, with the Detroit inset drawn from them.

items.title: S59, the Federal Reserve's unemployment projections
items.answer: S59 adds where the unemployment rate stood: its fourth-quarter average for 2021 to 2024, the projections' own measure, drawn before the fan.
items.what_changed: A second file, the fourth-quarter averages derived from the monthly rate the guide already holds. 2025 has no average, since October 2025 was not collected, and its column is drawn empty.
items.why: A fan of projections reads only against where the rate started.

items.title: S54 and S55, rent against renters' income
items.answer: S54 and S55 draw the Census Bureau's own measure of rent burden, median gross rent as a share of household income with its margin, in place of a ratio the studio worked out.
items.what_changed: The first file divided a year of median rent by the median income of all households, owners included. The file now carries the Bureau's table B25071 with its margin, beside median rent and renters' median income.
items.why: The studio's ratio mixed owners' income into a renters' measure and carried no margin.
items.recommendation: Approve S54 and S55 as drawn.
items.built: The same file rebuilt from tables B25071, B25064 and B25119 (research ledger P7-030).

items.title: S41, the plain table
items.answer: S41's table shows the 2023 survey alone, the question it answers. The House and Senate votes stay in S01 and S61.
items.what_changed: The plan's five rows mixed the survey's shares with the two chambers' votes.
items.why: A plain table should answer one question; the votes came three years after the survey and are on a bill with a second provision the survey never asked about.

plan_row.said: S01's survey shares and votes as a five-row table.

items.title: S20, homeownership by age
items.answer: S20 reads a second file with the Census Bureau's published margins for its 2015 and 2025 rates, so its title claims the rise for householders under 35 only because it passes its margin.
items.what_changed: A margins file beside the planned rates file, and a note that prints each change's margin.
items.why: Rule 14.9 lets a chart single out a survey change only past its margin; the under-35 rate rose 2.0 points against a margin of about 0.8.

items.title: Changes the data lead made to the data plans before anything was fetched
items.answer: Seventeen changes, five to the rounds 1 and 2 plan and twelve to the round 3 plan, each made before the research lead fetched the data, so the plan rows already carry them. They are listed so you can see where the specimens differ from the coverage plan you approved.
items.what_changed: Each row gives the change in a line.
items.why: Each keeps the form and tier and fixes a period, a source, a grouping or a rule the drawing needs.
